walkthroughs.body_html:
The Living World — a core area of GCSE Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

The Living World brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with The Living World.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between biotic and abiotic components of an ecosystem?
options: Biotic and abiotic both refer to types of soil.
Biotic means animals and abiotic means plants.
El Nino is the name of a specific hurricane that hit Mexico.
Biotic components are all living organisms (plants, animals, microbes); abiotic components are non-living factors (climate, soil, water, light, rock).

mcqs.q: What happens during an El Nino event?
options: Biotic and abiotic both refer to types of soil.
El Nino is the name of a specific hurricane that hit Mexico.
El Nino is when the ocean gets colder near Peru.
Trade winds weaken, warm water that normally pools in the western Pacific spreads east, disrupting weather patterns globally — drought in Australia, floods in South America.

mcqs.q: How do humans affect the carbon cycle?
options: By burning fossil fuels (releasing stored geological carbon to the atmosphere) and deforestation (reducing the biosphere store and releasing carbon).
Biotic and abiotic both refer to types of soil.
Humans affect the carbon cycle by eating plants.
Humans only affect the carbon cycle by breathing out CO2.
